entries.name: The Campaign in One Paragraph
entries: Perrin Cardon genuinely wants to restore the city his family founded, rebuild the Cardon fortune, and make Bellweather vibrant again. Before the campaign began, a presence he believed to be the {@b Spirit of the City} offered him “the power he would need to make the city his family founded vibrant again.” Perrin accepted. The spirit is actually {@b Tyren}, an ancient emerald dragon imprisoned beneath Varen Keep inside a magical prison called the {@b Radiant Cage}. Tyren can project his mind beyond the prison but cannot free his body. Perrin becomes the perfect vessel because his sincere civic ambition sits on top of an unrealized hunger for power. Perrin first uses Tyren’s gift to inspire cooperation and investment. He then organizes Bellweather’s criminals so their activity can discredit the Council and make Perrin look like the leader the city needs. Tyren hijacks that connected criminal network as his first successful experiment in controlling many minds at once. Perrin discovers what is happening, repeatedly chooses not to expose it, and eventually decides that direct control works better than influence. Tyren intends to scale the experiment from one criminal network, to one city, to every mind in the world.

entries.name: What This Campaign Is About
entries: The campaign is about {@b power becoming easier to justify each time it works}.

Perrin does not begin by wanting to enslave Bellweather. He begins by wanting people to care, invest, cooperate, and stop allowing a struggling city to fail. The first uses of his supernatural influence produce real benefits. That matters.
His corruption follows a simple progression:
{@b influence → manipulation → coercion → direct control}
Tyren never needs to implant Perrin’s desire for power. He only recognizes it before Perrin does and keeps rewarding it.
Perrin’s internal progression should remain equally simple:
{@b “I can help them choose what is best.”} {@b “I need enough authority to fix this.”} {@b “People keep getting in the way of what Bellweather needs.”} {@b “Why should they be allowed to refuse?”}
The supernatural and political stories are the same story. Tyren’s domination and Perrin’s increasing belief that he deserves control reinforce each other.

entries.name: What This Campaign Is Not About
entries: The campaign is no longer a district-by-district reclamation checklist.
Bellweather still changes. Old streets reopen. Trade improves. Properties return to use. The existing map remains valid. Every named place remains part of the world.
The characters now go somewhere because {@b a threat, clue, person, consequence, relationship, or player choice leads there}. They do not go merely because that location is the next block to clear.

Not every monster serves Tyren. Not every crime is part of Perrin’s plan. Not every tragedy was secretly caused by the central villain. Independent problems are important because they make Bellweather feel larger than one conspiracy.

entries.name: Canon at the Start of Session 4
entries: Session 4 begins {@b the next morning at Ledger House} after Session 3. Do not replay the Council meeting or ask the party to accept Kellan’s Well again.
The party consists of {@b four level-4 player characters}.
The following facts are already true:

items: The party survived the Slums and Blackstone Temple events as actually played.
The Blackstone captives were freed.
Tal Rusk and the guards with him were killed.
The Council possesses the coded Iron Covenant ledger, Pepper’s spyglass, and the compass recovered during the earlier adventures.
Bishop Brann’s reliquary was returned, and the party received the established reward.
The Council has already moved into and begun cleaning up the Slums.
Caleb’s body has already been found there with his head smashed.

Jarrock told Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin that Pepper killed Caleb. They reported the allegation. Pepper’s attempt to bluff created uncertainty, but the Council had enough circumstantial evidence to impose consequences.
Pepper is under {@b house arrest at Ledger House}, supervised by Brakkus. She may leave with Brakkus or on authorized Council business.
Pepper must complete {@b five mandatory Council missions} or go to jail. {@b Kellan’s Well is Mission 1 and is unpaid for Pepper. Missions 2–5 are paid normally.}
The rest of the party is paid normally for Kellan’s Well.
The party has already accepted the Kellan’s Well assignment.

entries.name: Session 3 Council Canon
entries: Use the people the players actually met, not obsolete source descriptions.

{@b Ulric Evern} is a human in his late fifties or early sixties, with silvering dark hair, a neat beard, conservative expensive clothing, a signet ring, and immaculate boots. He represents administration, budgets, procedure, and institutional continuity.

{@b Wern Ursen} is an elf: tall, lean, visibly scarred, and built like a career soldier. He wears practical plate marked with Bellweather’s crest. He thinks in terms of security, logistics, and survivability.

{@b Bishop Brann} is an older dwarf with a broad gray-white beard worn in braids, clerical robes over mail, a holy symbol, warm eyes, and scarred working hands. He is an experienced healer and priest rather than a ceremonial official.
{@b Perrin Cardon} is a human in his thirties or forties, exceptionally well dressed, polished, charming, and deliberately approachable. His public desire to make Bellweather prosperous is sincere.
{@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFASOC} remains the Ledger House anchor and established ally. Use his actual-play portrayal and relationships as authoritative.

entries.name: Core Recurring Cast
entries: Keep the recurring cast small. Temporary encounter NPCs may exist, but do not promote them into campaign principals unless actual play makes them important.

rows: Ledger House anchor; protector; grounded observer
Immune to direct control. His divine aura and a deeply anchored identity shaped by past trauma make Tyren unable to take the wheel.
Willing vessel. Believes Tyren is the Spirit of the City. Begins by using influence; eventually embraces direct control.
Ancient emerald dragon imprisoned in the Radiant Cage. Wants eventual control of every mind.
Immune to direct control. His devotion and the identity he built after childhood trauma make his mind exceptionally anchored.
Not secretly evil. His harsh but understandable responses to danger make him a plausible suspect and useful political foil.
Not secretly evil. Represents rules, budgets, records, and limits Perrin increasingly resents.
Resistant but not immune. He is so constitutionally incapable of accepting anything without evaluating whether it is a good deal that Tyren cannot hold him for long.

entries.name: Portraying the Core Cast
entries: These profiles are meant to be enough to pick an NPC up after several weeks away from the campaign and immediately know how to play them. Do not read them aloud. Use the physical details, cadence, habits, and pressure responses as table cues.

entries.name: Brakkus Ledgerhelm
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Brakkus is a broad-shouldered, scarred half-orc in late middle age whose physical confidence is obvious even when he is doing something mundane. He dresses like an innkeeper rather than a retired champion and does not advertise his old power. His hands are large, nicked, and steady. He tends to occupy doorways, corners, or the end of a bar where he can see the room without appearing to watch it.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Low, dry, and economical. Brakkus rarely uses three sentences when one will do. He lets silences sit instead of filling them. His humor lands as a flat observation rather than a joke he expects people to laugh at.

{@b Mannerisms.} He wipes the same section of bar while listening, checks a room with his eyes before responding to trouble, and often answers a foolish question only after deciding whether the asker genuinely wants an answer. When he is worried, he gets quieter rather than louder.

{@b What he wants.} Ledger House stays safe. People who need shelter get it. The party grows capable enough that they do not need him to solve their problems. He cares much more about whether ordinary people are getting hurt than whether a Council policy is elegant.

{@b What he knows.} Brakkus knows people, rumors, practical consequences, old adventuring habits, and what fear looks like. He does not know Perrin's hidden bargain or Tyren's plan until evidence reaches him. Do not turn him into an exposition machine.

{@b Under pressure.} Brakkus becomes frighteningly calm. He puts himself between danger and civilians, gives short instructions, and acts without theatrics. If the party makes a bad decision, he will tell them so, but he does not confiscate their agency.

{@b Relationship with the party.} He has moved past treating them as random customers. He notices when they are hurt, tired, lying, avoiding a subject, or pretending something did not bother them. He is protective without becoming paternalistic.
{@b Tyren interaction.} Tyren cannot take control of Brakkus. Brakkus may still be lied to, outmaneuvered, frightened for other people, or politically boxed in. His immunity is not omniscience.

entries.name: Perrin Cardon
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Perrin is a human in his thirties or forties, exceptionally well dressed without looking gaudy. His clothing is fitted, expensive, and always appropriate to the room. His hair is deliberately styled, his boots polished, and even after a bad night he presents himself as if he expected to be seen. He makes wealth look tasteful rather than ostentatious.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Warm, articulate, and conversational. Perrin prefers "we" and "Bellweather" to "I." He is good at making a person feel as though their concern was already part of his thinking. Early in the campaign, this is mostly genuine.

{@b Mannerisms.} He remembers names, turns his full attention toward whoever is speaking, and lowers his voice when he wants a conversation to feel private. When control is slipping, he straightens a cuff, smooths a sleeve, or becomes a little too precise about wording. Late in the campaign, he begins finishing other people's thoughts for them.

{@b What he wants.} Perrin truly wants Bellweather prosperous, admired, safe, and important again. He also wants the Cardon name restored. Beneath both is the desire he initially cannot admit: he wants to be the person whose decisions become reality.

{@b What he knows.} Early Perrin knows only that the Spirit of the City gives him unnatural influence. After Kellan's Well and Koven House he knows the Spirit is acting independently through the network. Savin and Marren force him to confront increasingly ugly explanations. Do not let him know the full dragon truth before the campaign reveals it.

{@b Under pressure.} Perrin argues rather than threatens. He reframes criticism as impatience, impracticality, or failure to understand the stakes. The more corrupted he becomes, the less willing he is to accept that another person's refusal might be legitimate.

{@b Relationship with the party.} Perrin should like them when they are useful, but that cannot be the whole relationship. He can admire competence, remember favors, resent humiliation, and sincerely believe they are helping build the city he loves. Their opinion of him should matter to him until very late.
{@b Portrayal progression.} Early Perrin persuades. Mid-campaign Perrin steers. Late Perrin decides. The change should happen in sentence structure before it happens in costume or villain speeches.

entries.name: Tyren
entries: {@b Presence before the reveal.} Tyren first exists as sensation, certainty, dream imagery, and a voice that seems to know Bellweather from the inside. He should not sound demonic. The "Spirit of the City" persona is patient, civic-minded, intimate, and almost reasonable.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Calm, measured, and utterly certain. Tyren does not rant. He speaks as though disagreement is an inefficiency rather than an insult. When speaking to Perrin, he often uses Perrin's own values and vocabulary: duty, prosperity, safety, unity, restoration, waste.

{@b Mannerisms without a body.} Repeated phrases appear in different mouths. Several people pause at the same moment. Someone answers a question before it is finished. A crowd turns its attention together. These are more effective than constant disembodied whispering.

{@b Physical reveal.} When finally seen beneath Varen Keep, Tyren is enormous even by dragon standards: a deep emerald body scarred by old bindings, chains and radiant sigils embedded around the prison architecture, eyes alert rather than feral. The shock should be that the calm voice the party has heard belongs to this ancient creature.
{@b What he wants.} Tyren believes individual will is the source of conflict, waste, fear, delay, and suffering. His answer is not conquest for tribute. It is permanent coordination under himself.

{@b How he sees Perrin.} Perrin is not a friend. He is not merely a pawn either. Tyren values him as the first willing conduit who proved that consent can open paths the Cage cannot close. Tyren rewards Perrin because rewarded ambition keeps opening doors.

{@b Under pressure.} Tyren becomes more direct, not more emotional. He treats resistance as a technical problem. His most unsettling moments should sound like diagnosis: "You are tired because you continue to choose separately."
{@b Do not play him as omniscient.} He knows what reaches his network. Anchored minds, protected conversations, distance, broken nodes, and deliberate countermeasures can deny him information.

entries.name: Bishop Brann
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Brann is an older dwarf with a broad gray-white beard worn in practical braids. Clerical robes sit over mail rather than replacing it. His holy symbol is well used, not decorative. His eyes are warm; his hands are scarred working hands, the hands of someone who has actually carried the wounded, dug graves, and repaired things.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Warm, plain, and patient. Brann is comfortable asking one difficult question and waiting for the answer. He does not sound like a sermon unless he is actually preaching.
{@b Mannerisms.} He checks injuries while people talk. He tends to stand close enough to be reassuring without crowding. When something angers him morally, his hands become very still.

{@b What he wants.} People protected before institutions are protected. He accepts that authority and force can be necessary, but he keeps asking who pays the cost and whether the person making the decision will bear any of it.

{@b The old wound.} As a child, Brann watched his sister murdered by a gang. That event did not turn him into a crusader obsessed with gangs. It shaped his refusal to let violence, fear, or hatred dictate what kind of man he would become. His devotion grew around that decision.

{@b Under pressure.} Brann gets simpler. He stops debating abstractions and names the person who will be hurt by the proposed action. He will stand against Perrin publicly if necessary, but he does not enjoy political combat.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Tyren cannot directly control Brann. This should become increasingly important once other civic leaders begin behaving with eerie agreement. Brann can still be deceived or manipulated through concern for other people.

entries.name: Wern Ursen
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Wern is a tall, lean elf with visible scars and the posture of someone who spent much of his life in armor before anyone gave him a Council chair. His plate is practical, maintained, and marked with Bellweather's crest. He does not dress to look ceremonial.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Short declarative sentences. He asks concrete questions: how many, how long, which road, who is holding the gate, what happens if this fails. He has little patience for vague optimism.

{@b Mannerisms.} Wern automatically notices exits, sight lines, bottlenecks, and how many armed people are in a room. He folds maps along existing creases and dislikes paperwork that hides the decision being made.

{@b What he wants.} Bellweather survives. Roads stay open. Civilians are not slaughtered because leaders were afraid to look severe. He has seen hesitation kill people and therefore tends to overvalue decisive action.

{@b Under pressure.} Wern's instinct is to tighten control: checkpoints, patrols, curfews, hard perimeters, clear chains of command. Sometimes he is right. Sometimes he goes too far. Do not secretly make him Tyren's willing agent to simplify the politics.
{@b Relationship with the party.} He respects competence, preparation, and people who can explain a plan in operational terms. He may disagree sharply with them and still trust them in a fight.

entries.name: Ulric Evern
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Ulric is a human in his late fifties or early sixties with silvering dark hair, a neat beard, conservative expensive clothing, a signet ring, and immaculate boots. He looks like someone who expects civic rooms to have rules and has spent decades learning them.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Measured and formal without being pompous. Ulric uses exact words, dates, sums, and obligations. He dislikes rhetorical shortcuts because he expects today's shortcut to become tomorrow's precedent.

{@b Mannerisms.} He straightens papers before reading them, turns a signet ring once when thinking, and asks who has authority to do a thing before discussing whether it is desirable. His irritation appears as increased precision rather than raised volume.

{@b What he wants.} Bellweather's institutions to survive the people currently occupying them. He believes power should be recorded, reviewable, funded, and limited enough that a competent successor can inherit it.

{@b Under pressure.} Ulric reaches for procedure. This can look cowardly when speed matters, but it is also the exact instinct that resists Perrin's argument that good intentions justify unreviewable power.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Unlike Brakkus and Brann, Ulric is vulnerable. If Tyren controls him later, make the evidence procedural: a signature he cannot remember making, an order in his phrasing that violates his own process, a sealed document filed in the wrong sequence.

entries.name: Jord
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Jord looks like a traveling cleric who has spent enough time around merchants, caravans, and adventurers to know the price of nearly everything. His clothing is practical and repaired rather than shabby, and he carries his possessions with the careful organization of someone who hates replacing things unnecessarily.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Friendly, skeptical, and transactional in the funniest possible way. Jord can turn a theological question into a discussion of terms without realizing he has done it. He is not greedy so much as constitutionally incapable of accepting a proposition before identifying the catch.
{@b Mannerisms.} He checks coin by habit, asks what something cost, and reacts to an obviously bad bargain with the same offended expression other people reserve for blasphemy.

{@b What he wants.} Good deals, useful work, decent company, and outcomes where everyone can plausibly say they got something worthwhile. He is capable of generosity, but he prefers generosity to be intentional rather than the result of being fooled.
{@b Under pressure.} The comedy drops quickly. Jord becomes practical and protective. When danger passes, the bargaining instinct returns almost immediately.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Jord is anchored but not immune. Tyren can force one brief {@spell command}-style action on a failed Wisdom save, but cannot hold him. Some deep part of Jord's mind keeps asking, "What are the terms?"

entries.name: Lessa Dorn
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Lessa is a lean, weathered half-elf whose clothing and gear look chosen for fieldwork rather than Council offices. She carries maps rolled too tightly, usually has charcoal or graphite on at least one finger, and looks at damaged streets the way a builder looks at a problem that should already have been fixed.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Direct, clipped when irritated, and much warmer when discussing practical work. Lessa does not soften criticism for rank.
{@b Mannerisms.} She points with whatever is already in her hand, marks corrections on maps while other people are still talking, and checks routes twice when someone else says "it should be fine."

{@b What she wants.} Survey crews protected, routes accurately documented, and decisions made by people who understand the actual ground conditions. Her anger at inadequate protection is professional before it is personal.

{@b Pepper relationship.} Lessa reported what Jarrock told her because that was the responsible thing to do. She does not need to become Pepper's prosecutor. Her opinion can change if Pepper behaves responsibly across the five missions, but she will not pretend Caleb's death stopped mattering.

entries.name: Kav Orin
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Kav is a halfling surveyor with a compact field kit, sturdy boots, and the permanent look of someone who has recently crawled under, over, or through something inconvenient. He is less visibly severe than Lessa but no less observant.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Quieter than Lessa and more likely to ask one clarifying question than make a speech. His humor is dry and often arrives after a tense moment rather than during it.
{@b Mannerisms.} Kav checks distances by eye, taps a pencil against his map case when thinking, and tends to move a half-step away from arguments that are becoming performative.

{@b What he wants.} Finish the work, get people home alive, and avoid turning every field problem into a political battle. He is more willing than Lessa to let behavior over time change his view of someone.
{@b Pepper relationship.} Kav believes the allegation was serious enough to report. He is not eager to punish Pepper beyond what the Council already imposed. He watches what she does next.

entries.name: Kerrik
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Kerrik is an aarakocra with travel-worn feathers, a lean frame, and the restless posture of someone more comfortable moving than sitting through a long conversation. When he comes to Ledger House about Elise, he looks as though he rehearsed the conversation several times and disliked every version.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Usually quick and blunt. Around Pepper he becomes controlled because anger and need are competing for the same space.
{@b Mannerisms.} His wings shift when he is irritated, and he looks toward exits when a conversation becomes too emotional. He has to make himself maintain eye contact with Pepper.
{@b What he wants.} Elise alive. Everything else is secondary in that scene. He does not want absolution, revenge, or a second trial.
{@b Relationship with Pepper.} Caleb was his closest friend. Kerrik can believe Pepper killed him and still come asking for help because Caleb's daughter matters more than Kerrik's pride.

entries.name: Mara
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Mara is a human woman carrying grief badly but functionally: tired eyes, practical clothes, hair put back because she has more important things to do, and the posture of someone who has been awake too many nights beside a sick child. She is not theatrically broken.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Direct. She has thought about what she needs to say and refuses to decorate it. When angry, she gets more specific rather than louder.
{@b Mannerisms.} Mara keeps one hand near Elise whenever they are in the same room. She rarely looks away from Pepper first.

{@b What she wants.} Her daughter helped. She does not come to Ledger House to forgive Pepper, understand Pepper, or make Pepper feel guilty. Those things may happen around the scene, but they are not Mara's objective.

{@b Relationship with Pepper.} Mara believes Pepper murdered Caleb. Asking Pepper for help costs her something. Do not make that request sentimental or easy. If Pepper helps, Mara's gratitude and her grief can coexist.

entries.name: Elise
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Elise is a young human girl who looks more exhausted than visibly injured. The illness has left her pale, short-tempered from poor sleep, and intermittently confused. She is still a child with interests, preferences, and impatience; do not play her as a spooky oracle.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Most of the time she speaks normally. The disturbing moments are brief: answering a question no one asked, repeating a phrase from elsewhere in the city, or beginning an action and then stopping because she does not know why she started.
{@b Mannerisms.} She rubs at her temples when the network is loud, loses her place in conversations, and becomes embarrassed when adults stare after an episode.
{@b What she wants.} To feel normal, sleep, and have the adults stop talking around her. She should remain a person rather than evidence.
{@b Tyren relationship.} Elise is collateral damage, not a chosen vessel, prophecy child, or hidden agent. Tyren did not target Caleb's family.

entries.name: Perrin and the Spirit of the City
The Bargain
entries: Before the characters arrived, Perrin began experiencing dreams and impressions from beneath Bellweather. The presence knew details about the old city that Perrin believed no outsider could know. It spoke about forgotten streets, Cardon holdings, civic failures, and the city’s founders with intimate certainty.
It never introduced itself to Perrin as a dragon.
It presented itself as {@b the Spirit of the City}.
Its offer was simple:
{@b “I can give you the power you will need to make the city your family founded vibrant again.”}
Perrin accepted.
He initially understands the gift as supernatural influence: people listen more closely, trust more easily, become more willing to cooperate, and feel stronger attachment to Bellweather’s future.
That gift works.

Perrin uses it to encourage investment, cooperation, civic pride, and political support. He also permits the Cardon family to benefit. In his mind, there is no contradiction: a prosperous Bellweather and a restored Cardon fortune are evidence that he is repairing what was lost.

entries.name: Why Tyren Chose Perrin
entries: Perrin is unusually useful because two desires coexist inside him.
His {@b surface desire} is real: restore Bellweather and his family.
His {@b unrealized desire} is power: not merely the responsibility to make decisions, but the satisfaction of being the person whose decisions become reality.
Tyren does not create this flaw. He recognizes it.
Perrin mistakes wanting control for wanting responsibility.

entries.name: Tyren, the Bound Dragon
entries: Tyren is an {@b ancient emerald dragon}. Use the official {@creature Ancient Emerald Dragon|FTD} stat block from {@i Fizban’s Treasury of Dragons} when the final physical confrontation occurs, with the campaign-specific adjustments in Chapter 17.
Tyren’s defining quality is not greed for treasure. It is a belief that separate wills create waste, conflict, fear, and disorder. He wants a world operating under a single mind: his.
Bellweather is not his final objective.
Bellweather is the prototype.

entries.name: The Radiant Cage
entries: Fifty years ago Tyren nearly took Bellweather by turning its population into extensions of his own will. Soldiers obeyed orders no officer had issued. Families betrayed one another without understanding why. Civic leaders repeated the same reassurances while the city’s institutions ceased behaving independently.
A small number of people could hear Tyren’s pressure without becoming his puppets. Later records call them {@b the Unturned}.

The Unturned discovered that killing Tyren’s physical body would not reliably end the threat. His consciousness had already spread through too many dominated minds, and they feared that destroying his body would simply leave his will anchored elsewhere.
They used the Radiant Well in a one-time ritual whose magical principles resemble {@b Imprisonment} and {@i {@spell soul cage}} on a scale far beyond an ordinary spell.
The ritual did three things:

items: {@b Bound Tyren’s body beneath Varen Keep.} His enormous physical form was chained inside a chamber built around the deepest accessible focus of the Radiant Well.
{@b Dragged his dispersed consciousness home.} The ritual pulled most of Tyren’s psychic presence out of the population and forced his mind back into his own living body.
{@b Locked body, soul, and name together.} Tyren could no longer permanently abandon his flesh for another host while the Cage remained intact.

entries: The Radiant Cage never made Tyren unconscious. It prevented physical escape and sharply limited his reach.
For decades Tyren could do little more than dream outward.
Then he learned to whisper.
Perrin answered.
A willing connection was the flaw the original jailers never designed the Cage to stop.

entries.name: How the Cage Fails
entries: Every mind Perrin successfully influences becomes a temporary path through which Tyren can push farther outside the Cage. One person is almost nothing. A coordinated criminal network is useful. A city trained to move according to shared impulses is transformative.

The final stage of Tyren’s plan requires the Radiant Well. He intends to reverse the original binding: instead of using the Well to pull his consciousness back into one body, he will use it to project his consciousness outward into an enormous network of minds.
Perrin eventually believes opening the Well fully will give him unrestricted access to the Spirit’s power and allow him to make Bellweather permanently orderly and prosperous.
That act opens the Radiant Cage.

entries.name: Anchored Minds and Tyren’s Control
entries: Tyren’s control is telepathic and supernatural. It uses the rules language of existing D&D enchantment effects so it behaves consistently at the table.

The campaign’s one major premise-specific rule is that Tyren must establish a psychic connection before his control can function. This is why a {@item Ring of Mind Shielding} blocks Tyren completely: a creature wearing the ring cannot receive Tyren’s unwanted telepathic contact, so Tyren cannot establish the connection required for his control.

entries.name: Ordinary Minds
entries: Tyren’s influence over ordinary NPCs escalates over the campaign.

{@b Influence — Suggestion model.} Early effects behave like {@spell suggestion}: Wisdom save, Charmed on a failure, achievable instruction, no obviously self-destructive order. Perrin believes this is the power he was given.
{@b Crowd Influence — Mass Suggestion model.} Once the criminal network is connected, Tyren can affect groups in ways modeled on {@spell mass suggestion}.

{@b Direct Domination — Dominate Person model.} Late in the campaign Tyren can directly operate ordinary humanoids through an effect modeled on {@spell dominate person}. This is never the mechanic used on player characters or Jord.
These are supernatural abilities, not literal spellcasting. Use the referenced spells for saves, behavioral boundaries, and duration unless a chapter states otherwise.

entries.name: Anchored Minds
entries: Some people possess an unusually fixed sense of self. Trauma is one path to that state, but not the only one. Faith, temperament, moral clarity, and deeply internalized identity can create the same resistance.
An anchored mind can be pressured, deceived, frightened, tempted, or socially manipulated normally. Tyren simply cannot maintain direct supernatural control over it.

entries.name: Player Characters and Jord — Resistant, Never Puppeted
entries: The PCs and Jord are resistant rather than immune.
{@b Hard campaign rule:} Tyren can never place a PC or Jord under anything stronger than a one-turn {@b Command-like} effect.
When a chapter calls for Tyren to seize an anchored mind:

items: ask for a {@b Wisdom saving throw} without explaining the source unless the characters have already learned what is happening;
on a success, nothing is compelled;
on a failure, give a brief one-word or one-action imperative modeled on {@spell command};
the effect lasts for {@b one turn / one compelled action only};
control immediately returns to the player;
never use this to force a PC to attack an ally, expend a major limited resource, reveal a secret, make a lasting roleplay decision, or perform obviously suicidal behavior.

entries: Tyren can seize the wheel for a moment. He never gets to play someone else’s character.

Do not begin using unexplained PC Wisdom saves early in the campaign. The first player-facing use should occur only after the story has escalated far enough that the phenomenon itself becomes a clue, recommended in Chapter 11.

entries.name: Why the PCs Resist
entries: Do not turn these into mechanical diagnoses. They are narrative anchors.
{@b Jarrock:} intense past trauma has left a mind that instinctively rejects intrusion and coercion.
{@b Aaron:} his history with domination makes another will trying to own him something his identity violently resists.
{@b Pepper:} her mind does not organize itself in the predictable patterns Tyren expects. He can force a momentary opening but cannot hold it.
{@b Arunem:} an unusually pure and uncomplicated moral center gives Tyren very little internal contradiction to exploit.
{@b Jord:} Jord lives for a good deal. At a fundamental level, his mind evaluates terms before accepting them. Even supernatural certainty runs into the same internal response: {@i What’s the catch?}

entries.name: Brakkus and Bishop Brann — Immune
entries: {@b Brakkus} is effectively immune to Tyren’s direct control. His divine aura and an identity reinforced by severe past trauma leave no stable foothold for Tyren.

{@b Bishop Brann} is also effectively immune. When he was a child, he watched his sister murdered by a gang. His immunity does not come from suffering itself; it comes from the person he deliberately became afterward. His devotion, moral discipline, and refusal to let violence dictate who he would become have made his sense of self extraordinarily difficult to displace.
Tyren can lie to Brakkus and Brann. He can threaten people they love. He can manipulate circumstances around them. He cannot directly take their actions away.

entries.name: The Historical Fall: What the Players Can Learn
entries: Do not hand the party one clean history of Tyren. The old records are damaged, censored, contradictory, and written by people who did not fully understand what was happening.
Use fragments such as these across Savin Keep, Marren Library, Rellan lore, and Varen Keep:
{@b “By the seventh day, even the watch answered with one voice. Orders passed without messenger or horn.”}
{@b “There were still some who heard him and would not turn.”}
{@b “The Unturned entered the chamber because none other could approach him and remain themselves.”}
{@b “His flesh was chained beneath the Keep, but iron could not hold his will.”}
{@b “The Well drew him home. Flesh, thought, and name became one again.”}
{@b “Bind the flesh. Break the reach.”}
{@b “So long as the Cage holds, let no voice answer the one beneath.”}
The important conclusions arrive in layers:

items: Something once coordinated people who should not have been coordinated.
It could take control of people.
A few people could resist it.
Those resistant people trapped it rather than killing it.
The trapped being is Tyren.
The prison is connected to the Radiant Well.
Tyren is an ancient emerald dragon beneath Varen Keep.

entries: Do not reveal Step 7 early.

entries.name: “No Cause for Alarm” Motif
entries: Use the phrase sparingly. It should accumulate meaning rather than become a joke.
Recommended beats from this point forward:

items: {@b After Kellan’s Well:} an official Council notice describes coordinated disturbances as contained and tells residents there is no cause for alarm.
{@b Savin Keep historical record:} the party finds the same civic phrase in a notice issued shortly before Old Bellweather collapsed.
{@b During Perrin’s rise:} Perrin uses the phrase publicly while insisting that isolated crime and political disagreements do not threaten the city’s progress.
{@b Late Bellweather:} the city becomes unnaturally orderly under mental control while official notices insist there is no cause for alarm.
{@b After the finale:} use one final callback only if it fits what actually happened. Do not force a canned closing line.

entries.name: Campaign Progression
entries: The party was promised a campaign through {@b level 16}. Preserve that promise.

rows: Marren Library and associated city investigation
Regional network: first major regional success

entries: The Mansion District and regional locations remain fully usable without each requiring an automatic level. They provide player-selected routes, allies, clues, resources, and consequences.

rows: Slums, Blackstone, Council consequences, Iron Covenant ledger
Separate groups act under one command system
Pay off Blackstone ledger; expose the criminal network
First records of the old takeover and the Unturned
Reveal Tyren's nature and Bellweather's old denial
First PC/Jord {@spell command}-style pressure; Tyren controls a crowd
Perrin knowingly chooses direct control because it works
Brann's immunity becomes visible; world remains larger than Tyren
Tyren identified as an imprisoned ancient emerald dragon
Bellweather is revealed as Tyren's prototype; allies and evidence
Perrin turns state power against the party
Perrin opens the Cage; guaranteed Tyren dragon fight
Koven House / Iron Covenant operation broken
Zennar betrayal survived and Bellweather return resolved

entries.name: Running Bellweather Between Adventures
entries: Ledger House remains the emotional anchor. Keep returns short unless the players want to linger.
After each major adventure:

items: Show one concrete change in Bellweather.
Put one familiar person in front of the party.
Show one consequence of the party’s previous choice.
Surface one or two live problems rather than announcing “the next chapter.”
Advance Perrin only when the party can see some result of his growing influence.

entries: Brakkus is not a quest dispenser and should not know hidden villain plans. He notices people, patterns, and changes in the city.

data.name: Chapter 5: Delving into Kellan’s Well

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/kellans_well.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/kellans_well.webp}
{@b Recommended level:} 4 {@b Expected milestone:} 5 {@b Likely table time:} 1–2 sessions

entries.name: Modern Running Sheet

rows: Establish that separate groups are being coordinated and point the investigation toward Koven House without revealing Perrin or Tyren.
Enter the old waterworks, stop runners, recover command/supply evidence, identify the common organizer.
Observe, infiltrate, descend openly, follow a courier, negotiate with lower-ranking crews, or attack.
The coordination clue cannot be lost. Failure changes preparedness, injuries, or escaped personnel.
Mission 1 of 5. Pepper receives no pay; the other PCs receive the normal Council reward. Pepper is legally permitted to leave Ledger House because this is Council business.
Someone has standardized the behavior of groups that normally do not cooperate.

entries: {@i Use the existing Kellan’s Well map and established geography.}

{@b Encounter purpose:} Investigation first, combat second. The party should leave knowing that separate groups are using one command system and that the Iron Covenant is involved.  {@b Whole-site opposition:} 5–8 low-tier humanoid combatants distributed through the site, one local {@creature Veteran|XMM}-style warden, and environmental threats from the existing waterworks.  {@b Surface:} 3 {@b Scouts} + 2 {@b Guards}, split between groups that visibly do not belong together.  {@b Underground pressure:} 2 {@b Scouts} or equivalent ranged defenders using cover; one environmental creature such as a {@creature Gray Ooze|XMM} or {@creature Carrion Crawler|XMM} only if pacing needs a nonhumanoid threat.  {@b Command room:} Warden using {@creature Veteran|XMM} or {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM} plus 2 {@b Guards} and 2 {@b Scouts}. Defenders surrender, flee, or bargain when the warden falls or half the force is down.  Do not run every creature at once.

entries.name: Rewards and Treasure
entries: Use {@b 250–400 gp} in mixed valuables, two useful consumables, and command/supply records. The evidence is more important than the cash.

rows: {@creature Gray Ooze|XMM}, {@creature Carrion Crawler|XMM}, or {@b Swarm of Rats}
{@creature Spy|XMM} if a mobile courier is needed

entries.name: Session 4 Opening
entries: Begin the next morning at Ledger House after the completed long rest and level-up.
Do {@b not} replay the Council acceptance scene.

Pepper’s house arrest remains in force. Brakkus does not need to escort her to Kellan’s Well because the expedition itself is authorized Council business. He makes clear that returning somewhere other than Ledger House afterward without Council permission would violate the terms.

Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin may be present outside or near Ledger House with a survey packet for the expedition. Their presence is intentionally awkward. They know what Jarrock told them about Caleb and they reported it. Neither needs to lecture Pepper. Their job is to hand over current route markings and leave the moral tension sitting at the table.
Lessa is professional and cool. Kav is uncomfortable but practical.

entries.name: What the Council Knows
entries: The Council already knows that multiple armed crews around Kellan’s Well are using identical hand signals, color marks, and timing. The crews do not appear to belong to one gang.
The Council wants answers to four questions:

items: Who is coordinating them?
What are they moving through the old waterworks?
Where do their instructions come from?
Can the underground route be kept from becoming a supply corridor into Bellweather?

entries: Do not introduce a “Boss” title as if the party should already understand it. The mystery begins with coordination.

entries.name: 1. Surface Approach
entries: The well house and nearby ruins are being watched by two small crews that dress differently and carry different local gang markers. Their behavior is the important clue: they use the same watch changes, the same hand signal for “strangers,” and the same fallback route.
Characters who spend ten minutes observing automatically notice the shared system.
A successful Wisdom (Perception), Wisdom (Insight), or Intelligence (Investigation) check can reveal more quickly that one crew waits for the other to acknowledge every movement before acting.
If the party approaches openly, one runner attempts to reach the underground junction on round 2 of any fight.
{@b Encounter.} Use 3 {@b Scouts} and 2 {@b Guards}, split between the two crews. They retreat if badly outmatched.

entries.name: 2. Well Chamber
entries: The stairs descend into old waterworks reinforced with newer timber. Crates near the entrance carry ordinary merchant brands, but the shipping chalk uses the same crossed-line system already encountered in earlier adventures.
A careful examination reveals a second mark hidden inside one crate: a small cross formed by four black iron nails.
This is an {@b Iron Covenant} mark.
The party does not need a check to recognize it if they have been shown the Blackstone ledger or symbol. Otherwise, the Council can identify it after the expedition.

entries.name: 3. Bow Gallery
entries: A side chamber overlooks the approach. Archers use cover and withdraw toward the junction after one or two volleys.
Use the existing maintenance-pit terrain from the current adventure rather than an arbitrary trap. Loose stone and a visible cracked edge telegraph the danger.

entries.name: 4. Junction
entries: This is the chapter’s essential clue room.

Three tunnels meet beneath a wall covered in chalk schedules. The crews are identified by {@b colors and symbols rather than gang names}. Different groups are being assigned shifts from one common schedule.
Characters who inspect the board automatically learn:

items: at least four separate crews have used the same command structure;
supplies are collected at Kellan’s Well and moved to a location referred to only as {@b HOUSE};
the command notation matches shorthand found in the coded Iron Covenant ledger held by the Council.

entries: A successful Investigation check adds that “HOUSE” is probably a permanent headquarters rather than a person.

entries.name: 5. Barracks
entries: Off-duty fighters include members of different crews. They are not fanatics.
Questioned separately, they tell similar stories:

items: they were offered better pay if they followed the shared schedule;
disputes between gangs suddenly became “bad for business” and stopped;
orders arrive through Covenant couriers;
nobody they know has met the person ultimately paying for the coordination.

entries: One frightened fighter says something stranger: a companion recently woke in the middle of the night, walked to the junction, changed the schedule, and returned to bed with no memory of doing it.
Treat this as unsettling color, not proof of possession.

entries.name: 6. Command Room
entries: Do not create another recurring mastermind. Use an {@b Iron Covenant Warden} represented by a {@creature Veteran|XMM} or {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM}.

entries.name: Portraying the Warden
entries: The Warden is a competent local operator, not a cultist and not a cackling villain. Dress the Warden in practical layered armor with a rain-dark coat, a key ring, and chalk or ink marks on the fingers from maintaining patrol boards. The voice is controlled and managerial: short instructions, no speeches, no ideological language. The Warden is visibly more bothered by {@b orders appearing outside the chain of command} than by the criminality of the operation itself.

When questioned, the Warden keeps trying to understand what the party already knows before answering. When frightened, the Warden glances toward the satchel and the nearest escape route. If defeat is obvious, self-preservation beats loyalty.
The Warden understands the criminal structure but not Tyren.
The Warden knows:

items: the Covenant has been paid to make separate crews cooperate;
instructions and money flow through Koven House;
several instructions have appeared in the system without the Warden knowing who issued them;
the Warden assumes someone higher in the Covenant is bypassing local command.

entries: The Warden tries to escape with a satchel if defeat becomes likely.
{@b Encounter.} Warden plus 2 {@b Guards} and 2 {@b Scouts}, adjusted for the party’s condition.

entries.name: 7. Stores and Escape Route
entries: The stores contain {@b 250–400 gp} in mixed criminal proceeds, two useful consumables, and mundane supplies.
The important treasure is documentary:

items: Covenant routing notes;
a list of four gang symbols assigned common shift colors;
a coded reference to {@b Koven House};
a payment token issued through a legitimate commercial intermediary whose ownership trail eventually brushes Cardon-connected money without proving Perrin ordered anything.

entries: Do not put Tyren’s name, a dragon symbol, or Perrin’s signature here.

entries.name: Tactical Response
entries: If the alarm is raised, defenders try to hold the junction long enough to burn routing notes and move the command satchel. They do not create infinite reinforcements.
The party can win the chapter by any of the following:

items: seize the command documents;
capture the Warden;
turn one of the crews;
follow a fleeing courier far enough to identify Koven House;
preserve enough physical evidence for the Council to decode the ledger connection.

entries.name: Return to Bellweather
entries: The Council now has its first credible evidence that the Iron Covenant is coordinating criminals who should be competitors.
Ulric wants warrants and documentation before expanding the investigation.
Wern wants Koven House watched immediately and argues that waiting gives the Covenant time to relocate.
Brann asks whether the lower-ranking criminals are being coerced and whether anyone has reported memory loss or unusual behavior.
Perrin publicly supports a careful investigation. He appears genuinely concerned.

entries.name: DM Truth: Perrin’s First Off-Ramp
entries: Perrin recognizes more in the report than he admits.

He organized the criminal coalition through intermediaries because he wanted crime to become visible, coordinated, and politically damaging to the Council. He intended eventually to support a crackdown and emerge as the person who restored order.
He did {@b not} order the strange schedule changes or memory-loss behavior.
For the first time Perrin understands that the Spirit of the City is independently using the network he assembled.
He could confess.
He does not.
This is Perrin’s first major corruption choice.

entries.name: Pepper: Mission 1 Complete
entries: If Pepper returns as ordered and does not abandon the mission, mark {@b Mission 1 of 5 complete}.
Pepper receives no Council payment for this mission. The other three PCs receive the established Council pay.

Lessa or Kav can be present when completion is recorded. Keep the interaction short. Their continuing presence lets Pepper’s legal consequence remain part of the world without making every session about her crime.

entries.name: No Cause for Alarm Beat
entries: Within a day, the Council posts a public notice intended to prevent panic:

{@b PUBLIC NOTICE:} Irregular criminal activity near Kellan’s Well has been contained. Council investigators are reviewing evidence of coordination between several local crews. Trade and ordinary business may continue. {@b There is no cause for alarm.}
The notice is not sinister. That is why it works.

entries.name: Milestone
entries: Advance the party to {@b level 5} when the Kellan’s Well evidence is secured and the Koven House lead is established.

data.name: Chapter 6: Koven House

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/koven_house.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/koven_house.webp}
{@b Recommended level:} 5 {@b Expected milestone:} 6 {@b Likely table time:} 1–2 sessions

entries.name: Modern Running Sheet

rows: Pay off the Iron Covenant ledger and reveal that the criminal network is centralized enough for someone else to use it.
Infiltrate or assault Koven House, seize Covenant ledgers, free prisoners, break the local command structure.
Stakeout, secret entry, captured courier, roof approach, service tunnels, negotiation, or direct assault.
Essential ledgers survive in at least one cache. Failed stealth changes enemy positioning rather than deleting the story.
Mission 2 of 5. Paid normally if completed.
The Iron Covenant deliberately unified multiple gangs, but some orders are now appearing without any Covenant officer claiming responsibility.

entries: {@i Use the existing Koven House map, concealed routes, roof access, courtyard, and service corridors.}

{@b Koven House is an Iron Covenant headquarters.} The house is a prepared criminal command site, not a generic thieves' guild.  {@b Whole-site force:} 1 {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM}-style Covenant factor, 3–4 {@b Spies}, 4 {@b Thugs}, and 2 {@b Scouts}, distributed through the mansion.  {@b Typical scene:} 1 {@creature Spy|XMM} + 2 {@b Thugs} using a secret route, trap, or crossfire. They withdraw once one ally drops unless protecting evidence.  {@b Final command-room scene:} Covenant factor + 2 {@b Spies} + 2 {@b Thugs}. If the party arrives depleted, remove one Spy rather than reducing every enemy's hit points.  The Covenant prioritizes destroying records, escaping through service corridors, and protecting its patronage structure over fighting to the death.

entries.name: Rewards and Treasure
entries: The portable criminal hoard is worth about {@b 1,500 gp} in coin, gems, jewelry, and negotiable valuables. Much of the property in the house belongs to identifiable victims.
Recommended permanent rewards: {@b one +1 weapon or +1 shield}, plus 2 spell scrolls of 3rd level or lower and 2 consumables.

rows: {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM} with Iron Covenant flavor

entries.name: The Iron Covenant at Koven House
entries: Koven House is {@b an Iron Covenant headquarters}.
The Covenant is not a dragon cult and does not worship Tyren. Its leadership believes it has built a profitable criminal coalition with political protection and unusually reliable financing.

Perrin’s original purpose was political. Through intermediaries, he encouraged the Covenant to bring competing gangs into one structure. Increased organized crime would make the Council look incapable. When the city became frightened enough, Perrin intended to support the crackdown, destroy the network, and step forward as the person who restored order.
Tyren saw a different opportunity: Perrin had gathered a large number of compromised, connected people into one communication system.
Koven House is where Tyren begins treating that system like a nervous system.

entries.name: Getting the Job
entries: The Kellan documents and the coded Blackstone ledger point toward the same place after Council clerks compare routing shorthand.

Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin can assist by placing old property boundaries over the recovered delivery routes. Their work establishes that multiple routes terminate at the same mansion compound: Koven House.
Ulric authorizes a warrant once the documentary connection is strong enough.
Wern wants the party to move before the Covenant burns records.
Perrin agrees that immediate action is justified. This is not an act. He genuinely wants this Covenant node broken now that he knows the Spirit is issuing instructions through it without him.

entries.name: Table-Ready Opposition
entries: Spread the defenders across the house rather than fighting them all at once.
Use approximately:

items: 4 {@b Spies};
4 {@b Thugs};
2 {@b Scouts};
1 {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM} as the Covenant Factor.

entries: Adjust counts for party resources. Defenders use hidden routes, cover, doors, and retreat plans. They bargain or flee once the command structure is clearly broken.
Do not create another campaign-long villain here. The Factor is a local operator.

entries.name: Interactive Traps
entries: Preserve the old house’s prepared-defense identity, but every hazard needs a tell and a countermeasure.

rows: old horizontal cut marks; new tension wire
DC 14 Perception notices. DC 14 Dexterity with thieves’ tools disables. Trigger: DC 14 Dex save, 3d6 slashing, half on success.
DC 14 Perception. Trigger: DC 14 Con save, 2d6 poison and Blinded until end of next turn; half and no blindness on success.
Characters can shore it up or move carefully. Trigger: DC 14 Dex save, 3d6 bludgeoning, half on success; rubble becomes Difficult Terrain.
Initiative starts when sealed. Three rounds to escape, block nozzles, or prevent ignition. Burning creatures take 2d6 fire at end of turn until out or fire suppressed.
DC 14 Dex save or Restrained. Action and DC 12 Strength check, or cutting the net, frees a target.
DC 14 Dex save or fall 10 feet, 1d6 bludgeoning, Prone.

entries: A trap that sounds an alarm advances the house response instead of simply adding more damage.

entries.name: 1. Outer Yard
entries: The mansion exterior looks better maintained than surrounding ruins. Someone has money, workers, and reasons to preserve it.
Characters watching for an hour see couriers arrive separately and leave by different routes. The couriers wear no common uniform.
One detail is shared: every courier touches a black iron-nail cross fixed beneath the gate lintel before being admitted.

entries.name: 2. Auxiliary Buildings
entries: Use these for surveillance, a hidden service entrance, or a neutral creature/squatter that has learned to avoid the Covenant.

If using the existing quickling encounter seed, keep the quickling {@b unnamed and nonrecurring}. Respectful characters can learn that people inside sometimes walk through the house at night “like they’re dreaming.”

entries.name: 3. Service Corridors
entries: The Iron Covenant uses concealed corridors to move between rooms, attack from advantage, and retreat.
A character who captures a map, spends ten minutes searching a known section, or follows a withdrawing defender can discover a route without needing a single pass/fail roll.
The first important cache contains duplicates of Kellan’s shift schedules and the same color coding.

entries.name: 4. Prison and Blackmail Rooms
entries: The Covenant keeps debtors, informants, and blackmail targets here. Most prisoners know only ordinary criminal information.

One prisoner reports something useful: the Covenant Factor recently punished a lieutenant for issuing an order the Factor swore he never gave. Three witnesses heard the Factor’s voice give the instruction.
The Factor blamed impersonation.
This is the first evidence that the impossible coordination may involve more than couriers and paperwork.

entries.name: 5. Ledger Room
entries: The ledgers establish the Covenant’s structure.
The essential discoveries are automatic once the room is secured:

items: competing gangs were paid bonuses for operating under shared schedules;
the Covenant financed neutral meeting sites and compensated gangs for settling old feuds;
money entered the network through ordinary-looking commercial channels;
one channel leads to a Cardon-connected intermediary, but the paper trail stops before proving Perrin ordered crimes;
several payments were authorized using a code {@b not found anywhere in the Covenant’s own key}.

entries: That unknown code appears only on instructions that produced no obvious profit: moving people to particular buildings, changing patrol routes, gathering crowds, or keeping specific streets busy at specific times.
These are Tyren’s experiments.

entries.name: 6. Covenant Factor
entries: The Factor uses a {@creature Bandit Captain|XMM} stat block and has 2 {@b Spies} nearby if the party reaches the command room before breaking the house response.

entries.name: Portraying the Factor
entries: The Factor looks more like a prosperous fixer than a street criminal: good coat, clean hands, expensive pen, and a small visible piece of Iron Covenant ironwork worn as if it were a business credential. The Factor speaks softly and assumes everyone has a price, a fear, or a practical reason to compromise.

This NPC should feel dangerous because of {@b competence and information}, not because of theatrical cruelty. The Factor knows names, debts, schedules, who can be leaned on, and which local disputes can be turned into leverage. The unnerving crack in that confidence is the command problem inside the Covenant: orders have been given in familiar voices without the supposed speakers remembering them.

When pressed on those incidents, the Factor becomes defensive in a very specific way—less "that is impossible" and more "someone has compromised my system." The Factor still believes there is a human explanation.
The Factor knows the following:

items: an outside patron paid the Covenant to unify criminal operations;
the patron never appeared personally;
the arrangement was supposed to be profitable and politically protected;
somebody has recently begun issuing orders through the network without paying and without using recognized Covenant authority;
people who receive those orders often insist afterward that they made the choice themselves.

entries: The Factor assumes a rival has compromised the organization.
If captured alive, the Factor can identify the commercial intermediary but cannot identify Perrin.

entries.name: 7. Command Cache
entries: A hidden command cache contains the best evidence and one disturbing object: a page where several different hands have copied the same sentence in nearly identical wording.
{@b We know where we are needed. We will be there.}
None of the writers remember being told to write it.
Do not label this “mind control” for the players.

entries.name: Treasure
entries: The house contains approximately {@b 1,500 gp} in portable criminal wealth, much of it identifiable as stolen property.

Use one memorable permanent uncommon item, two useful spell scrolls of 3rd level or lower, and two consumables. Returning identifiable property improves the party’s standing with victims and merchants.

entries.name: Resolution
entries: Koven House is broken when the Factor is captured, killed, driven out, or loses the ability to coordinate the Covenant cell and the party secures the ledgers.

The Iron Covenant survives as an organization unless the party takes extraordinary steps. What breaks here is its central Bellweather headquarters and the political usefulness of this particular network.

entries.name: DM Truth: Perrin’s Second Off-Ramp
entries: Perrin now has documentary confirmation that the Spirit is issuing commands through the organization he created.
He also sees a benefit.

The Covenant becomes easier to destroy because frightened criminals are behaving predictably. Perrin can publicly support the raid and privately tell himself that the Spirit merely helped clean up the mess Perrin intended to clean up eventually.
He does not confess.
His rationalization changes from {@b “I didn’t authorize that”} to {@b “the result was still useful.”}

entries.name: Pepper: Mission 2 Complete
entries: If Pepper completes the authorized mission and returns to Ledger House, mark {@b Mission 2 of 5 complete}. She is paid normally from this point forward.
Lessa and Kav may verify the recovered property routes or assist the Council in documenting the house. They do not become investigators of Caleb’s death; that matter is already known and adjudicated.

entries.name: Milestone
entries: Advance the party to {@b level 6} after Koven House is broken and the party understands that the coordination extends beyond one location.

data.name: Chapter 7: Savin Keep

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/savin_keep.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/savin_keep.webp}
{@b Recommended level:} 6 {@b Expected milestone:} 7 {@b Likely table time:} 1–2 sessions

entries.name: Modern Running Sheet

rows: Transform the current criminal mystery into a historical mystery: Bellweather has seen impossible coordination before.
Reach the keep, survive or bypass bound defenders, recover the final garrison records, stop hostile agents from destroying them.
Research passwords, use the old oath, parley with spirits, force entry, or exploit conflict between old defenders and current raiders.
Historical clues have redundant sources. Missing one clue changes context, not whether the party can continue.
Old Bellweather’s defenders recorded the same one-mind behavior fifty years ago and referred to a few resistant people as the Unturned.

entries: {@i Use the existing Savin Keep map and island geography.}

Preserve the undead oath/password structure and the historical-record objective. Do not turn Savin Keep into a long undead attrition crawl.  {@b Interior defenders:} small groups of {@b Skeletons}, {@b Zombies}, {@b Specters}, and one {@creature Wight|XMM} acting as the last command element.  {@b Environmental creature:} one {@creature Ochre Jelly|XMM} or {@creature Gray Ooze|XMM} where the source geography supports it.  {@b Record-burning strike team:} 1 {@creature Veteran|XMM}, 2 {@b Bugbears} or equivalent hard hitters, and 4 {@b Guards/Scouts}. Their goal is to burn records and escape; they withdraw if the commander falls or half the force is defeated.

entries.name: Rewards and Treasure
entries: Keep the {@b Potion of Heroism}, the historical records, and either one {@b +1 weapon} or {@b +1 shield}. Convert excess armory wealth to about {@b 500 gp} in salvage and ceremonial equipment.

entries.name: Why Savin Keep Matters Now
entries: The Koven ledgers contain routing references to old harbor records and a pre-fall military code. Ulric’s clerks identify Savin Keep as the last place that code was formally used.
The Council is not sending the party to “reclaim the next district.” It wants the records before the Iron Covenant or another interested party destroys them.
Wern is particularly interested because the same coordination pattern could represent a military threat.
Brann is interested because descriptions of memory loss and involuntary behavior resemble possession or enchantment.
Perrin wants the records recovered too. He is now quietly desperate to understand what the Spirit really is, though he does not tell the party that.

entries.name: The Old Defender Oath
entries: Preserve the existing challenge-and-response/password structure. The fragments {@b Lux}, {@b Shestnik}, and {@b Samosud} remain useful old garrison terms.
Characters can find enough fragments through records, plaques, and the approach to bypass some undead guardians. The passwords are advantages, not gates that can stall the adventure.

entries.name: 1. Shore and Gate
entries: Old remains near the landing include a corroded medallion and part of a watch schedule.
Recent tracks show that another small team arrived within the last two days. Their objective is not occupation; they are looking for records.
The undead defenders respond to the old password or to clear evidence that the visitors are acting under Bellweather authority.
Use {@b Skeletons}, {@b Zombies}, {@b Specters}, and one {@creature Wight|XMM} across the chapter rather than a mass battle.

entries.name: 2. Courtyard
entries: The bound defenders still follow the final orders they received fifty years ago.
If combat occurs, one spirit repeatedly says:
{@b “Hold until the Unturned reach the lower chamber.”}
This is the first use of the historical term. Do not explain it yet.

entries.name: 3. Barracks Archive
entries: A hidden diary from the final week before Bellweather fell describes soldiers receiving contradictory orders.
Useful fragments:
{@b “By the seventh day, even the watch answered with one voice. Orders passed without messenger or horn.”}
{@b “We changed the countersign twice. It did not matter. Men who had not attended the briefing knew it before sunset.”}
{@b “Three in the east barracks still hear the pressure and remain themselves. Chaplain calls them Unturned.”}
The diary never says dragon.

entries.name: 4. Old Chapel
entries: The final chaplain’s spirit can be used if the party approaches respectfully. Do not make the spirit another ongoing NPC.
The spirit remembers fragments, not a lecture.
It can establish:

items: the enemy was called {@b Tyren} in sealed military reports;
Tyren could “speak through” citizens and soldiers;
a few people could resist;
those people went beneath Varen Keep with civic mages and priests;
after that night, the voices stopped;
the survivors refused to record the full ritual in one place.

entries: The spirit points toward {@b Marren Library} as the repository that received copies of pre-fall magical research.

entries.name: 5. Command Stone
entries: The binding focus for the undead defenders remains active.

Speaking the release phrase found in the chapel ends the ordinary defenders’ duty and allows them to rest. If the party instead destroys the focus, the same result occurs but damages one archive room.
A sealed report beneath the stone contains the campaign’s first explicit Tyren line:
{@b TYREN — CONTROL EVENT. Civilian spread accelerating. Standard command compromised. Use Unturned personnel for all communication regarding Varen.}
No creature type is listed.

entries.name: 6. Record-Burning Strike Team
entries: Before the party can leave, a small current-day strike team attempts to burn the archive.
Do not identify them as Tyren cultists. They are paid criminals and mercenaries using an Iron Covenant route.
{@b Encounter.} 1 {@creature Veteran|XMM}, 2 {@b Bugbears} or equivalent hard hitters, and 4 {@b Guards/Scouts}. Their objective is fire and escape, not killing every PC.
The strike leader carries no supernatural symbol. Payment came through the same unknown command code seen at Koven House.
This is Tyren protecting old information without Perrin ordering it.

entries.name: No Cause for Alarm Historical Beat
entries: Among ordinary civic papers is a public circular dated shortly before Bellweather’s fall:

{@b PUBLIC ASSURANCE:} Reports of erratic watch conduct and contradictory instructions remain isolated. Civic services continue under established authority. Residents are asked to disregard irresponsible rumors. {@b There is no cause for alarm.}
Do not underline the coincidence for the players.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Returning with the records changes the investigation.
Ulric accepts that the coordination is not merely a modern criminal innovation.

Wern begins treating the problem as an internal-security threat and advocates stronger emergency powers, more checkpoints, and tighter command discipline. His response is severe enough to be genuinely debatable.
Brann focuses on the Unturned and asks what made them different.
Perrin reacts carefully. He asks more questions about the term Tyren than he should logically need to, then catches himself.
If challenged, he explains that anyone hearing the report would want to understand the threat.

entries.name: DM Truth
entries: Perrin asks the Spirit about the name {@b Tyren} in private.
Tyren tells him that the old rulers feared the true spirit of Bellweather and branded it a threat because it could make the city act with one purpose.
Perrin does not fully believe this explanation.
He chooses to keep listening anyway.

entries.name: Pepper: Mission 3 Complete
entries: Completing the mission marks {@b Mission 3 of 5}.

Lessa or Kav can be present when the recovered maps and records are logged. Their attitude should reflect what Pepper has actually done during the mandatory missions rather than reset to hostility every time.

entries.name: Milestone
entries: Advance to {@b level 7} when the Savin records are secured and the party knows that the present coordination resembles a historical event associated with the name Tyren.

data.name: Chapter 8: Cardon Weavehouse

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/cardon_weavehouse.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/cardon_weavehouse.webp}
{@b Recommended level:} 7 {@b Expected milestone:} 8 {@b Likely table time:} 1–2 sessions

entries.name: Modern Running Sheet

rows: Let Perrin’s original dream visibly succeed: Cardon wealth and Bellweather prosperity begin returning together.
Recover Cardon and civic records, resolve current occupants/hostile holdouts, secure valuable machinery and assets.
Support Perrin’s claim, impose public conditions, negotiate with occupants, divide records/assets, or challenge ownership.
The family and civic records are recoverable through multiple rooms and witnesses.
Perrin’s methods are producing visible good, making his rationalizations more persuasive to himself and to the city.

entries: {@i Use the existing Cardon Weavehouse map.}

The Weavehouse is about Perrin's restored inheritance becoming materially real. Use combat to put pressure on the ownership decision, not to bury it.  {@b Outer patrol:} 2 {@b Veterans} or 1 {@creature Veteran|XMM} + 2 {@b Scouts}.  {@b Main opposition:} 1 {@creature Gladiator|XMM}-style leader with 2 {@b Scouts} or 2 {@b Guards}. If the group reaches this fight fresh, add one {@creature Veteran|XMM}; otherwise keep the leader isolated enough that the party can negotiate or force surrender.  {@b Optional shrine / coercion scene:} 1 {@creature Priest|XMM} or {@creature Cult Fanatic|XMM} + 2 {@b Guards}, only if it serves the story.

entries.name: Rewards and Treasure
entries: The Cardon family cache is primarily {@b story property}, not free loot. Give the party a normal level-appropriate monetary reward, 2 consumables, and at most one uncommon/rare permanent item from the site.

entries.name: Why the Party Goes
entries: Savin’s records identify the Cardon Weavehouse as one of the sites where pre-fall emergency supply books, shipping ledgers, and old property archives were duplicated.
Perrin publicly asks the Council to authorize an expedition. His reasons are openly mixed:

items: the records may clarify the Tyren mystery;
surviving machinery could create jobs;
the building belongs to his family under old deeds;
restoring a major Cardon enterprise would bring capital into Bellweather.

entries: None of those claims is automatically false.
This is exactly why the chapter matters.

entries.name: Perrin’s Public Position
entries: Perrin does not hide that he wants his family property back.
He argues that Bellweather needs private investment, functioning businesses, and people willing to risk money on recovery. He promises to reopen the Weavehouse rather than leave it as a private ruin.
If the party challenges him on profiting from Council risk, he does not become sinister. He argues the point.

entries.name: 1. Approach
entries: The Weavehouse is occupied by a mixed group of squatters, hired guards, and opportunists using portions of the structure.
Separate people by behavior rather than species.

Some occupants will leave if offered safe passage. Some workers claim they have maintained machinery for years and deserve a share. A small armed faction intends to sell the contents and resists negotiation.

entries.name: 2. Loom Hall
entries: The main loom floor is dangerous because of weakened catwalks and partially functioning mechanisms.
Use environmental hazards rather than random monsters:

items: broken catwalk sections;
suspended weights;
jammed gear trains;
unstable stored dyes.

entries: A fight here should reward movement and creative use of machinery.

{@b Encounter option.} 1 {@creature Gladiator|XMM}-equivalent leader, 2 {@b Veterans}, and 2 {@b Scouts}, distributed between floor and catwalks. They surrender or flee when the leader falls and escape remains possible.

entries.name: 3. Worker Quarters
entries: Several current occupants are noncombatants who have been living in the building.
They know Cardon agents have already visited and offered employment if Perrin regains legal control.
Most of those offers are real.

This is one of the first visible examples of Perrin using influence for something that produces a genuinely positive result. People who were suspicious of him become enthusiastic after short private conversations.
Do not call for PC saves. The effect is on NPCs and should still look like charisma, hope, or politics.

entries.name: 4. Family Archive
entries: The archive contains Cardon deeds, partnership papers, and proof that the family once held substantial legitimate property.
It also contains emergency ledgers showing that the Weavehouse supplied food, cloth, and shelter during the first days of the old crisis.
Perrin can point to this history as evidence that the Cardons did not merely enrich themselves; they helped hold the city together.
A separate civic ledger references transfers to Marren Library during the last week before the fall.
That is the next major historical lead.

entries.name: 5. Hidden Cardon Reserve
entries: A family reserve of portable wealth survived behind a sealed wall.
Use a meaningful but controlled amount: {@b 2,000–3,000 gp equivalent} in coin, trade bars, gems, and negotiable records, plus one family heirloom magic item appropriate to the tier.
Legally, most of it belongs to Perrin under the recognized deed unless the party or Council successfully challenges that claim.
Recovering it materially changes Perrin’s circumstances.
This is the point where the Cardon fortune stops being a nostalgic ambition and becomes real economic power.

entries.name: The Ownership Decision
entries: The party does not decide Bellweather law by fiat, but its testimony and actions matter.
Possible outcomes include:

items: recognize Perrin’s full claim;
require compensation or tenancy rights for current workers;
place historical records in public custody while returning commercial assets to Perrin;
negotiate a mixed public/private operation;
challenge the claim and force a Council hearing.

entries: Perrin remembers how the party treats him here.
He does not need to become their enemy if they oppose him.

entries.name: Bellweather Changes
entries: Within weeks, if Perrin receives enough of the property, the Weavehouse reopens in some form.
Jobs appear.
Merchants invest.
The Cardon name becomes associated with visible recovery.
Perrin’s wealth and public approval increase together.
This is a success story.
That fact is essential to his corruption.

entries.name: DM Truth: Rewarding the Hidden Desire
entries: Tyren’s gift appears vindicated.

Perrin can now look at a functioning business, paid workers, increasing trade, and restored family wealth and conclude that his willingness to do what cautious people would not do is exactly why Bellweather is improving.
The hidden desire for power is no longer merely hidden. Perrin begins enjoying being the person who can make outcomes happen.

entries.name: Pepper: Mission 4 Complete
entries: Mark {@b Mission 4 of 5 complete} when the authorized objective is resolved and Pepper returns as required.

entries.name: Milestone
entries: Advance the party to {@b level 8} after the Weavehouse crisis is resolved and Perrin’s restored wealth becomes a visible part of Bellweather politics.

data.name: Chapter 9: Marren Library

entries.name: Maps
entries: {@link Player Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/player/marren_library.webp}
{@link DM Keyed Map|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/img/dm/marren_library.webp}
{@b Recommended level:} 8 {@b Expected milestone:} 9 {@b Likely table time:} 1–2 sessions

entries.name: Modern Running Sheet

rows: Reveal what Tyren can do without yet revealing what Tyren physically is. Finish Pepper’s five-mission Council sentence.
Preserve the archive, recover the Tyren material, stop a targeted theft/burning of records, decide who controls copies.
Work with scholars, Council, Cardon interests, or independent custodians; split priorities; protect records rather than simply clear rooms.
Core Tyren and Radiant Cage clues survive in more than one source.
Mission 5 of 5. Paid normally. Successful completion ends the mandatory mission sentence and house arrest.
Tyren can occupy living hosts; the Radiant Well was used to contain him; killing a host does not necessarily kill Tyren.

entries: {@i Use the existing Marren Library map and archive geography.}

The Library is a knowledge-and-control chapter. Books and records are the primary treasure and the possession reveal is the primary payoff.  {@b Guardians:} use 1–2 encounters from {@creature Animated Armor|XMM}, {@creature Flying Sword|XMM}, {@creature Specter|XMM}, {@creature Shadow|XMM}, {@creature Mimic|XMM}, {@creature Nothic|XMM}, or {@creature Gibbering Mouther|XMM}.
